I · Introduction

Did you know?

🌲 Mostly conifers

Most plants in this chapter are conifers: Christmas trees and their relatives.

🌰 Two kinds of cones

Every species here has pollen cones and seed cones.

🦕 A menu upgrade

Before seeds, animals had only leaves, stems and roots to eat, all much lower in nutrients than seeds.

🧬 Not one clade

These plants are usually called gymnosperms, but evidence shows they are not one complete clade.

Chapter opener: a pine cone

  • Pollinated pine cones with seeds developing inside are the equivalent of unripe fruits.
  • At pollination they were about 1 cm long, with scales spread apart so wind-borne pollen could settle near the ovules.
  • Mature cones are dry, tough and inedible.
  • Rare exception: Juniperus (juniper) cones are fleshy and edible.
II · Concepts: why seeds evolved

The problem with a spore-based life cycle

  • Vascular cryptogams (seedless vascular plants) alternate independent, heteromorphic generations: sporophyte and gametophyte live separately and look different.
  • A new sporophyte embryo depends on a tiny gametophyte for its start in life, so many new sporophytes perish.
  • It would be better if the embryo could use the leaves and roots of the parent sporophyte.
  • To do that, the megagametophyte and embryo must be kept inside the maternal sporophyte.

The genetic logic

GametophyteGrows from the parent’s spore, so all its genes match the maternal sporophyte.
New embryoShares half its genes with the maternal sporophyte.
ResultAny mutation that helps gametophytes or embryos survive raises the reproductive success of the maternal sporophyte, so natural selection favors it.
II · Concepts: why seeds evolved

Step 1: keep the megaspore at home

A–B · Megaspore released

A spore holds only a little food. Once it is shed, the parent cannot nourish or protect the gametophyte or the next sporophyte.

C–D · Megaspore retained

Mutations that reduce megaspore number and keep the megaspore in the sporangium are favored. The parent feeds and shields the gametophyte and embryo.

D · The embryo’s position

In gymnosperms the embryo sits inside megagametophyte tissue. In flowering plants the tiny megagametophyte is quickly replaced by endosperm.
II · Concepts: why seeds evolved

Step 2: a new problem and a simple fix

Problem

Retained megagametophytes sit high on the plant in strobili. Swimming sperm from microgametophytes on the soil surface cannot reach them.

Solution (Fig. 22-1E)

  • Megasporophylls are arranged in upright cone-like structures.
  • Wind carries microspores into the cone, where they germinate into microgametophytes.
  • Antheridia release sperm within 1–2 mm of the archegonia.
  • Fertilization itself changes little: a moist sporophyll replaces moist soil.

These changes produced the first seed plants: seed ferns * and early conifers of class Cordaitales *. Both are extinct, but their descendants live on.

Sperm deliveryWhere it occurs
Swimming sperm (still produced)Lines leading to cycads and Ginkgo
Nonmotile sperm carried to the egg by a pollen tube (growth of the microgametophyte)Lines leading to conifers and flowering plants
Pollen tube: growth of the microgametophyte that carries the sperm to the egg, so the sperm no longer need to swim.
II · Concepts: wood before seeds

Wood came first

  • Some lycophytes and horsetails had evolved vascular cambia on their own, but they made only rather slender trees.
  • In the new cambium, cells could divide radially and longitudinally, so the cambium grew in circumference as wood accumulated.
  • Result: trees as massive as giant redwoods, oaks and hickories.
  • This cambium probably arose just once, giving a monophyletic group of woody plants, the lignophytes.
  • Shortly afterward, seeds originated, giving the seed plants, the spermatophytes.
Lignophytes: woody plants (cambium grows in circumference)

Progymnosperms *

Wood present, but they still reproduced by spores, the way ferns do.
Spermatophytes: seed plants
Seed ferns * · cycads · conifers · Ginkgo · gnetophytes · angiosperms
Sequence to remember: wood → seeds. The plants living between the two origins were spore-bearing trees.
II · Concepts: relationships

Reading the seed-plant cladogram

1
Lignophytes (top bracket) = every woody plant on the tree.
2
Progymnosperms branch off first: Aneurophytales * and Archaeopteridales *. They are woody but have no seeds.
3
Spermatophytes arise at the black bar (more than 325 MYBP).
4
The “Gymnosperms” bracket covers cycads, conifers, ginkgos and gnetophytes (Ephedra, Welwitschia, Gnetum), but not angiosperms.
The chapter calls this “one recently proposed cladogram”: a model, a hypothesis, not a final answer.
II · Concepts: relationships

What is an unresolved polychotomy?

Original schematic based on Chapter 22 (concept from Fig. 22-2)
  • In Fig. 22-2, many groups emerge from the same point.
  • This does not mean they arose at the same moment. It means we lack the information to know the order in which the groups and their innovations arose.
  • One problem: DNA cannot be extracted from such long-dead fossils, so extinct groups such as seed ferns cannot be included in DNA analyses.
Cladistics review: a resolved tree shows sister groups. A polychotomy honestly shows what is still unknown.
II · Concepts: patterns

Two suites of characters

CharacterCycadophyte suiteConiferophyte suite
WoodManoxylic: a small amount of very soft, spongy, parenchyma-rich wood (Fig. 22-26)Pycnoxylic: hard, strong wood with little parenchyma (Fig. 22-3)
LeavesLarge, compoundSmall, simple
SeedsRadially symmetricalFlattened (bidirectionally symmetrical)
Found inCycads and their relativesConifers and their relatives
The coniferophyte syndrome probably evolved out of the cycadophyte syndrome, but as Fig. 22-2 shows, we are not yet certain.
Memory aid: mano- = loose (soft wood); pycno- = dense (hard wood).
II · Concepts: classification

Why “gymnosperms” is not a natural group

Old system (1800s)

One division, Spermatophyta, with two classes:
  • Gymnospermae: “naked ovules” on flat sporophylls (e.g., pine cones)
  • Angiospermae: flowering plants with carpels; fruits are mature carpels
If angiosperms evolved from some gymnosperm, “gymnosperms” leaves out some descendants. An incomplete group is paraphyletic, so class “Gymnospermae” should be abandoned.

Used in this book: 5 living divisions

① Cycadophyta ② Coniferophyta ③ Ginkgophyta ④ Gnetophyta (these 4 = “gymnosperms”) ⑤ Magnoliophyta (flowering plants)
Key extinct groups: progymnosperms *, seed ferns *
Original schematic based on Chapter 22. Use “gymnosperm” as a convenient informal label, not a clade.
III · Division Progymnospermophyta

Progymnosperms: wood without seeds * extinct

Rhyniophytesearly vascular plants
Trimerophytespseudomonopodial branching; first steps toward megaphylls
Three linesferns · horsetails · progymnosperms
  • Why the name? Some progymnosperms later gave rise to conifers, cycads and the other gymnosperms.
  • Like ferns and horsetails, they evolved megaphyllous leaves.
  • Just as significant was a vascular cambium with unlimited growth potential, producing both secondary xylem and secondary phloem, as early as 360 million years ago.
  • Some (e.g., Triloboxylon, Proteokalon) had a cork cambium that produced bark.
  • True woody trees: trunks up to 1.5 m in diameter and 12 m tall.
Progymnosperms = extinct, woody, spore-producing plants with a vascular cambium of unlimited growth. They had no seeds.
Learning Objective 2: progymnosperms combine advanced wood and leaves with simple spore reproduction.
III · Division Progymnospermophyta

Progymnosperm wood looked like conifer wood

  • Elongate tracheids, most with circular bordered pits
  • Little or no axial parenchyma
  • Tall, uniseriate rays (one cell wide) made of procumbent ray tracheids
  • Strong, good at conduction, able to support a large mass of leaves and branches
  • Almost indistinguishable from the wood of many living conifers
Ray tracheids: horizontal tracheids in the rays that allow rapid sideways conduction in the sapwood. Common in conifers; absent in flowering plants.
III · Division Progymnospermophyta

Table 22-1 · Two orders of progymnosperms

TABLE 22-1 Classification of Division Progymnospermophyta*
Order Aneurophytales
Family AneurophytaceaeAneurophyton, Eospermatopteris, Proteokalon, Protopteridium, Tetraxylopteris, Triloboxylon
Order Archaeopteridales
Family ArchaeopteridaceaeArchaeopteris, Callixylon

*All species of this group are extinct.

Why keep them apart from conifers?

  • Their wood was similar to conifer wood, but progymnosperms had no seeds or even ovule precursors.
  • Later species were heterosporous, yet megaspores were shed through longitudinal slits in the sporangia.
  • Seed plants instead keep the megaspore in an indehiscent (non-opening) sporangium.
Learning Objective 3: the two orders are Aneurophytales and Archaeopteridales.
III · Division Progymnospermophyta

Order Aneurophytales: the more relictual group

  • Examples: Aneurophyton, Protopteridium, Proteokalon, Tetraxylopteris, Triloboxylon, Eospermatopteris
  • Ranged from shrubs (Protopteridium, Tetraxylopteris) to large trees up to 12 m tall
  • All had a vascular cambium and secondary growth…
  • …but the primary xylem of the stem was a protostele, like that of rhyniophytes and trimerophytes.
  • Little webbing between ultimate branches: the “fronds” were branch systems, not true leaves. Planation and webbing had not yet evolved.
Descendants (Summary 4): Aneurophytales evolved into pteridosperms, cycads, cycadeoids and perhaps angiosperms.
III · Division Progymnospermophyta

Order Archaeopteridales: the more derived group

  • Archaeopteris: small trees with abundant wood and secondary phloem (text: up to 8.4 m; Fig. 22-4: about 6 m), flourishing ~360 million years ago across northern North America, Canada and Europe
  • Stem a siphonostele: pith surrounded by a ring of primary xylem bundles, much like modern conifers and dicots
  • “Fronds” were planated branch systems; the “leaflets” were spirally arranged simple leaves
  • Heterosporous, but megaspores were released, not retained, so no seeds. Gave rise to conifers.
IV · Evolution of seeds

Fossil evidence: Archaeosperma arnoldii

Why fossils are tricky: spores can be matched to their sporophyte only if trapped in an attached sporangium. Spores can be linked to gametophytes only when the gametophyte develops inside the spore wall. Retained megaspores make this easier.

Earliest known heterosporous progymnosperm: Chaleuria, Middle Devonian, about 390 million years ago.

  • Upper Devonian Archaeosperma: one megaspore mother cell → 1 functional megaspore + 3 aborted cells
  • Integument: a tissue layer around the megasporangium, extending upward as finger-like projections
  • Micropyle: a large hole in the integument through which sperm swam to the egg
  • Pollen chamber: a calm, wind-free space above the sporangium where pollen or spores settled
  • Cupule: partially fused telomes around each ovule, which may later have given rise to the carpel of angiosperms
IV · Evolution of seeds

How did the integument form? From sterile telomes

A · SeparateSporangia not grouped with sterile telomes
B · SurroundedOne megasporangium ringed by sterile telomes
Genomosperma kidstoni
C · Fused at baseTelomes fuse at their bases
G. latens
Fused to tipOne structure except at the tip
Eurystoma angulare

Fig. 22-8G, Stamnostoma hyttonense, is another fossil that matches the hypothesis.

Why it mattered:
  • The sheath of sterile branches trapped wind-blown microspores, at first anywhere on the megasporangium.
  • As the telomes fused to each other and to the megasporangium, the space at the top became the place where microspores settled: the pollen chamber.
  • The fused sheath = the integument, which will become the seed coat.
IV · Evolution of seeds

Pollen evolves too, and the “seed recipe” (LO 1)

At the same time, microspores were evolving into pollen grains: changes in the wall, in the method of germination and in the microgametophyte inside. By the Carboniferous (about 340 million years ago), four types of pollen were common, some with internal microgametophytes very similar to those of modern gymnosperms.
1 · RetainFewer megaspores; one functional megaspore kept in an indehiscent megasporangium (nucellus)
2 · WrapSterile telomes fuse into an integument
3 · CatchA micropyle and pollen chamber hold incoming pollen
4 · DeliverPollen with an internal microgametophyte; later a pollen tube (conifers, angiosperms)
= SeedEmbryo fed by the megagametophyte (or endosperm), supplied by the parent and protected by sporangium + integument

Based on the chapter text and Summary points 1–3.

V · Division Pteridospermophyta

Seed ferns * extinct: a grade, not a clade

  • Progymnosperms gave rise to the cycadophytes, in three divisions: Pteridospermophyta *, Cycadophyta (living) and Cycadeoidophyta *. (In “Pteridospermophyta,” the “p” is silent.)
  • Seed fern = any woody plant with fern-like foliage that bore seeds instead of sori on its leaves.
  • Many looked like tree ferns (but had wood); others were vines.
  • Earliest in the Upper Devonian; others appeared later.

Clade

All descendants of a common ancestor, whatever their level of evolution.

Grade

A level of evolution. Seed ferns are not all closely related, so they form a grade.
V · Division Pteridospermophyta

Inside a seed fern stem

  • Ancestry: evolved from Aneurophytales. The earliest seed ferns (Stenomyelon) had a three-ribbed protostele, as in Triloboxylon and Aneurophyton.
  • In later species (Stenomyelon, Calamopitys, Lyginopteris), central cells became parenchyma, giving a pith surrounded by a ring of vascular bundles, the arrangement found in all gymnosperms and angiosperms.
  • A long-lived vascular cambium made both xylem and phloem.
  • Manoxylic wood: tracheids long and wide, with several rows of circular bordered pits; rays many cells wide and very tall (large wedges of parenchyma).
  • Thick cortex with radial plates of sclerenchyma and secretory ducts. A cork cambium later formed bark, and the cortex was shed with the first bark.
TracheidsPit rows per radial wall
Seed ferns (long, wide)Several
Conifers (narrow)Only one or two
V · Division Pteridospermophyta

Fern-like leaves that bore seeds

  • Leaves were large, compound and planar, like true fern leaves in overall organization.
  • Their resemblance to fern leaves is analogous, not homologous: similar form, but not inherited from a common fern-leaf ancestor.
  • Ovule: a large megasporangium (nucellus) with vascular bundles running into it, and a vascularized integument attached only at the base.
  • Seeds could be huge: up to 11 cm long and 6 cm wide in Pachytesta incrassata.

LO 4 · Three features of seed ferns

  1. Woody plants with large, compound, fern-like leaves
  2. Seeds borne on foliage leaves, not in cones
  3. Manoxylic wood with a pith, plus a cortex with sclerenchyma plates and secretory ducts
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Conifers: big, familiar and successful

  • About 50 genera and 550 species; forests cover over 17 million km². In many of these forests, flowering plants occur only as herbs, shrubs or small trees in the conifers’ shade.
  • Giant redwood (Sequoiadendron giganteum): up to 90 m tall and 10 m in trunk diameter.
  • Never vines, herbs or annuals; never with bulbs or rhizomes.

LO 5 · Four features of conifers

  1. Always trees (moderate to gigantic) with solid, pycnoxylic wood and no vessels
  2. Leaves always simple needles or scales, mostly perennial
  3. Simple pollen cones and compound seed cones on every species
  4. Nonmotile sperm carried to the egg by a pollen tube

  • Cordaitales: the early conifers, among the first seed plants

  • Araucariaceae: in Agathis and Araucaria, leaves remain even on very old trunks

Connect to later slides

  • Sequoiadendron: the giant redwood (up to 90 m)
  • Podocarpus: fleshy, red fruit-like seed cones
  • Juniperus: fleshy, blue seed cones
  • Taxus: single seeds with a red, fleshy aril, and no ovulate cones
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Conifer leaves: simple, tough, long-lived

  • Never compound: always simple needles or scales, leathery, and most persist for many years
  • Simple venation: 1–2 long veins in needles; several parallel veins in scale leaves
  • Veins have an endodermis and transfusion tissue (transfusion parenchyma + cuboidal transfusion tracheids with circular bordered pits), which moves materials between vascular tissue and mesophyll
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Conifer wood and phloem: no vessels, no sieve tubes

  • Wood almost entirely tracheids (no vessels, as in Archaeopteris); tracheids so narrow that only 1–2 rows of pits fit
  • Growth rings: wide, thin-walled early (spring) wood vs narrow, thick-walled late (summer) wood
  • Rays thin and tall, with ray parenchyma + ray tracheids; resin canals (pitch) run vertically and in rays
Phloem: sieve cells and albuminous cells, not sieve tube members (no sieve plates). A cork cambium makes thick bark that protects even against forest fires.
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Pines as a model: two kinds of shoots

  • Pine trees are monopodial: one main trunk bearing many branches.
  • Long shoots bear tiny, papery scale leaves.
  • In their axils grow short shoots, which produce the familiar long needle leaves (Fig. 22-13C).
  • Needles are xeromorphic (drought-adapted): thick cuticle, sunken stomata, cylindrical shape.
Look ahead: Ginkgo also has short shoots (bearing most of its leaves) and long shoots.
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Pollen cones are simple cones

Simple cone: a single, short, unbranched axis that bears microsporophylls directly. Microsporophylls are leaf-like structures that bear microsporangia.
  • Microsporangia dehisce and wind carries the pollen away.
  • Inefficient: only a small percentage lands on seed cones, and the rest die.
  • It works because conifers grow in dense forests, so each tree has hundreds of potential partners.
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Pine pollen: a tiny microgametophyte with wings

  • Microspore mother cells undergo meiosis to form microspores.
  • Each microspore develops endosporially (inside its own wall) into a small gametophyte of about four cells, including a generative cell.
  • The tube cell forms the pollen tube; the generative-cell line yields two nonmotile sperm.
  • Two air bladders add volume but almost no weight, so density drops and the pollen sinks slowly in air.
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Seed cones are compound cones

  • The cone axis bears cone bracts (true leaves), not sporophylls.
  • Each bract has an axillary bud that bears the megasporophylls.
  • In modern conifers the bud is microscopic and its megasporophylls are fused laterally into a flat ovuliferous scale bearing two ovules.
  • In larch, fir and Douglas fir, the scale is still distinct. In most conifers (e.g., pine) it is fused to the bract, which baffled early morphologists until fossils explained it.
VI · Division Coniferophyta · LO 6

Compare: simple pollen cone vs compound seed cone

Comparison summary (based on Chapter 22)
Pollen coneSeed cone
TypeSimpleCompound
Axis bearsMicrosporophylls directlyCone bracts (leaves), each with an axillary bud
SporophyllsLeaf-like, bearing microsporangiaMegasporophylls fused into an ovuliferous scale

Beyond conifers: cycad seed cones are simple (no bracts or axillary buds); gnetophyte pollen and seed cones are both compound.
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Inside the ovule

  • Each ovuliferous scale bears two ovules. Ovule = integument + nucellus (the actual megasporangium).
  • One megaspore mother cell → meiosis → 3 degenerate, 1 megaspore survives.
  • The nucellus does not open, so the megaspore is retained.
  • Free nuclear divisions form a coenocytic (multinucleate) megagametophyte with up to 7,200 nuclei; after up to a year, walls form.
  • Two or three archegonia, each with a huge egg packed with carbohydrate and protein.
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Slow fertilization, many embryos, one survivor

  • Pollen arrives before the egg is mature; more than a year may pass between pollination and fertilization.
  • A massive pollen tube digests its way through the nucellus. This is necessary because the megasporangium never opens. (Contrast mosses and ferns, whose archegonia are exposed to swimming sperm.)
  • All 2–3 eggs may be fertilized, but only one zygote develops into an embryo.
  • The suspensor pushes the proembryo deep into the megagametophyte. The suspensor can divide to form several embryos (cleavage polyembryony), but only one survives.
  • No double fertilization. The nutritive tissue is the haploid megagametophyte, often called “endosperm.”
VI · Division Coniferophyta

Putting it together: the pine life cycle

Original schematic based on Chapter 22 (pine). Seeds mix generations: 2n coat and embryo, n food tissue.
Cones in nature: usually woody, but fleshy and fruit-like in Podocarpus (red) and Juniperus (blue). Fir cones fall apart; others expand and drop their seeds; some open only when heated by fire.
VII · Division Cycadophyta

Cycads: not ferns, not palms

  • Often mistaken for ferns or young palms: stout trunk, tough pinnately compound leaves.
  • Most are under 1–2 m; Macrozamia can reach 18 m.
  • Trunk covered by bark and persistent leaf bases, which provide most of the support.
  • Stem like a seed fern’s: thick cortex with secretory ducts, a small amount of manoxylic wood (long, wide tracheids, massive rays) and a prominent pith with secretory canals.
  • Leaf veins have transfusion tissue like conifer leaves.
  • Today about 9–10 genera, ~100 species: scattered tropical survivors (Cuba, Mexico, Australia, southeast Asia, Africa) of a once larger, widespread group. Few tolerate freezing.
VII · Division Cycadophyta

Cycad reproduction: separate sexes, swimming sperm

Always dioecious

Pollen cones and seed cones grow on separate plants. Pollen cones are simple, with spirally arranged, shield-shaped microsporophylls bearing clusters of microsporangia.

Swimming sperm

Pollen forms a branched pollen tube and large multiflagellated sperm (hundreds of flagella) that swim to the egg.

Seed cones: relictual → derived

Cycas revoluta: loose leaf-like, pinnately compound megasporophylls, 6–8 ovules.
Zamia floridana: shield-shaped megasporophylls, 2 ovules, compact cone.
VII · Cycads vs seed ferns · LO 7

How do cycads differ from seed ferns?

Ancestry: seed ferns gave rise to cycads and cycadeoids (Summary 6).
VII · Division Cycadeoidophyta

Cycadeoids * extinct: cycad bodies, bisexual cones

  • Vegetatively almost identical to cycads, differing only in subtle details of stomatal complexes and leaf-trace organization.
  • On those features alone they would never be separated from cycads. Cones are the difference:
Comparison summary (based on Chapter 22)
CycadsCycadeoids *
Cone sexesSeparate pollen and seed cones on separate plantsOne cone holds both microsporophylls and megasporophylls
OvulesOn megasporophyllsStalked; integument extends into a long micropyle; thick fleshy scales between ovules

VIII · Division Ginkgophyta · LO 8

A whole division for one species: Ginkgo biloba

The “maidenhair tree” is the sole living species of its division. It is unusual enough to deserve one.

  1. Looks like a large dicot tree, with a stout trunk and many branches.
  2. Wood like conifers: no vessels and no axial parenchyma.
  3. Broad leaves with dichotomous venation, like seed ferns and cycads, not reticulate like dicots.
  4. Short shoots (bearing most leaves) and long shoots.
  5. Dioecious, gymnospermous, with no cones: naked ovules in pairs on a short stalk, and pollen in a catkin-like organ.
Also: Ginkgo keeps swimming sperm, like cycads, and its large ovules develop a three-layered seed coat.
VIII · Division Ginkgophyta

Ginkgo: a survivor with a smelly secret

🍂 Ornamental tree

Leaves turn brilliant yellow in autumn. Microsporangiate (“male”) trees are preferred, because the fleshy outer seed layer of megasporangiate (“female”) trees gives off butyric acid, which smells putrid.

🦴 Who ate the seeds?

The flesh-covered seeds must have been eaten by some animal that is now extinct (At the Next Level).
AncestryExact ancestors unknown; must have been a seed fern or a close relative. Fig. 22-2 proposes a common ancestor with cycads, but DNA analysis cannot include extinct seed ferns.
Mesozoic heydayAbundant, especially mid-Jurassic (~170 million years ago); fossil leaves and wood worldwide, even at high latitudes (Alaska, Canada, Siberia; Patagonia, South Africa, New Zealand).
DeclineBegan dying out early in the Tertiary. G. biloba and G. adiantoides persisted; G. adiantoides went extinct in the Pliocene.
IX · Division Gnetophyta · LO 9

Gnetophyta: three enigmatic groups

Gnetum · ~30 species

Mostly vines or small shrubs with broad, dicot-like leaves. Southeast Asia, tropical Africa, Amazon Basin.

Ephedra · ~40 species

Tough shrubs with reduced, scale-like leaves. Deserts of northern Mexico and the southwestern USA; dry South American mountains.

Welwitschia · 1 species

Short, wide stem and only two leaves, growing perennially from a basal meristem. Deserts of South Africa (per the chapter).
IX · Division Gnetophyta

Gymnosperms with vessels: are they kin to flowering plants?

Unusual features

  • Vessels in the wood, rare among gymnosperms
  • Compound pollen cones with small bracts (unlike all other gymnosperms)
  • Compound seed cones with extra tissue layers around the ovules (read as an extra integument, bract or sporophyll)
  • Distinctive spindle-shaped, ridged pollen, with fossils back to the Late Triassic. Organ fossils are only several million years old.
Anthophyte hypothesis: gnetophytes and flowering plants are sister clades with a common ancestor (“Division Anthophyta”).

Weighing the vessel evidence

Gnetophyte vesselsAngiosperm vessels
Evolved fromTracheids with circular bordered pitsScalariform tracheids
TimingPresent in all three generaAncestors were vessel-less; vessels evolved after flowers
So vessels probably arose independently and do not prove kinship. There are too few data to be confident: we do not yet know. Fig. 22-2 stays a hypothesis.

X · Summary

Chapter 22 in nine points

  1. In a seed, the embryo feeds on the megagametophyte (or endosperm), which the parent supplies; sporangium and integument protect it.
  2. In all modern seed plants the nucellus does not open, so a pollen tube delivers the sperm. Sperm are still motile in many seed plants.
  3. Progymnosperms arose from trimerophytes with a cambium of unlimited growth. Seed evolution began with them: first megaspore retention, then an integument.
  4. Archaeopteridales → conifers; Aneurophytales → pteridosperms, cycads, cycadeoids, and perhaps angiosperms.
  5. Conifers: diverse large trees with solid wood, simple pollen cones and compound seed cones.
  6. Seed ferns gave rise to cycads and cycadeoids. Key changes: pith, and ovules on unspecialized foliage leaves. Wood rich in axial parenchyma.
  7. Cycads: compound leaves, parenchymatous wood, simple seed cones with leaf-like megasporophylls.
  8. Ginkgo biloba, the sole living species of its division: dicot-like tree, but with dichotomous veins and naked ovules (no cone, no carpel).
  9. Gnetophytes: gymnospermous reproduction; Ephedra and Gnetum look like dicots; Welwitschia has two ever-growing leaves.

At the Next Level: research ideas

1 · Animals and gymnosperms

  • Birds cache conifer seeds and forget some, which then germinate far from the parent.
  • Red arils of Taxus and soft blue juniper cones attract animals.
  • Ginkgo’s fleshy seeds were likely eaten by an animal now extinct.
  • Cycads: mostly wind, but beetles have been found carrying pollen.

2 · Conifers in the last 100 million years

  • Giant redwoods now survive in just a few California valleys, yet were once abundant and widespread.
  • Earth cooled starting about 50 million years ago.
  • Redwoods show how refugia help species survive changing conditions: a gateway to conifer paleoecology.

3 · Cycad sperm cells

  • Large sperm with hundreds of flagella in a long spiral around half the cell.
  • Each flagellum needs a basal body, so hundreds must be made as each sperm matures.
  • An unusual corner of plant cell biology.

Knowledge check: think, then click

1
Why is “gymnosperms” not a natural group? Use the term paraphyletic.
If angiosperms evolved from some gymnosperm, the group “gymnosperms” includes that ancestor but leaves out some of its descendants (the angiosperms). An incomplete group like this is paraphyletic, so “gymnosperm” is only a convenient informal label.
2
Could an indehiscent megasporangium have evolved before integument-penetrating pollen tubes? What problem would arise? (RQ 18)
Only if sperm still had a way in. A closed megasporangium with no opening would block swimming sperm from the archegonia, so there would be no fertilization. Early ovules solved this with a micropyle and pollen chamber. In conifers, sperm reach the eggs only because a pollen tube digests through the nucellus.
3
Progymnosperm wood looks like conifer wood. Why keep the two groups separate?
Progymnosperms had no seeds or ovule precursors. Even heterosporous species shed their megaspores through slits instead of retaining them in an indehiscent sporangium. Similar wood does not make them seed plants.
4
Why are seed fern leaves analogous, not homologous, to true fern leaves?
They are similar in form, venation and tissue structure (large, compound, planar), but they were not inherited from a common fern-leaf ancestor. Seed ferns came from a separate (aneurophyte) line, and their leaves bore seeds, not sori.
5
How does a simple pollen cone differ from a compound seed cone in conifers?
Pollen cone: one unbranched axis bearing microsporophylls directly. Seed cone: the axis bears bracts, and each bract’s axillary bud bears megasporophylls fused into an ovuliferous scale with two ovules, so it is a branched (compound) system.
6
Gnetophytes have vessels. Why doesn’t that prove a close relationship to flowering plants?
Their vessels evolved from tracheids with circular bordered pits, while angiosperm vessels came from scalariform tracheids. Angiosperm ancestors were also vessel-less, with vessels evolving after flowers. Vessels likely arose independently, so the anthophyte idea remains unproven.

Important terms: term check

Hide the definitions and try to define each term aloud.
angiosperms – flowering plants; ovules enclosed in carpels (fruits = mature carpels)
anthophytes – proposed sister-clade grouping of gnetophytes + angiosperms (unconfirmed)
compound cones – cones whose axis bears bracts, each with an axillary bud bearing sporophylls
cone bracts – true leaves on a seed-cone axis; each has an axillary bud
gymnosperms – seed plants with “naked” ovules on sporophylls; informal, paraphyletic group
integument – tissue layer around the megasporangium; becomes the seed coat
lignophytes – monophyletic group of woody plants (cambium grows in circumference)
long shoots – main elongating shoots; in pine they bear tiny papery scale leaves
manoxylic wood – small amount of soft, spongy, parenchyma-rich wood
micropyle – hole in the integument through which sperm (or a pollen tube) reach the egg
ovuliferous scale – fused megasporophylls of an axillary bud; bears two ovules
pollen chamber – calm space above the megasporangium where pollen settles
proembryo – cells pushed into the megagametophyte by the suspensor; become the embryo
progymnosperms – extinct woody, spore-bearing plants with unlimited cambium; no seeds
pycnoxylic wood – hard, strong, dense wood with little parenchyma
seed ferns – extinct woody plants with fern-like leaves bearing seeds; a grade
short shoots – shoots in the axils of long-shoot leaves; in pine they bear the needles
simple cones – one unbranched axis bearing sporophylls directly
spermatophytes – seed plants
suspensor – elongating early cells from the zygote that push the proembryo inward
